title: What is CSS?
summary: CSS controls how a web page looks and how its parts fit together.

subtopics.title: A rule
subtopics.explanation: A CSS rule has a selector and declarations. In `p { color: navy; }`, `p` selects paragraphs and the declaration sets their color. It is like an instruction with a target and a change. Braces hold the declarations together. A rule can contain several properties, such as color and line-height.

subtopics.title: Selectors
subtopics.explanation: A selector chooses which HTML elements receive a rule. `.notice` selects elements carrying the `notice` class. It is like putting the same label on several boxes. Use classes for reusable component styles, and keep selectors simple so a rule does not affect unrelated parts of the page.

subtopics.title: Properties and values
subtopics.explanation: A property names the visual setting, such as `color`, `padding`, or `display`; its value tells the browser what to use. For example, `padding: 1rem` adds space inside a box. It is like choosing a setting and then choosing its amount. Invalid values may cause the browser to ignore a declaration.

subtopics.title: The cascade
subtopics.explanation: The cascade decides which matching rule supplies a property when several rules apply. Importance, selector specificity, and source order all matter. It is like resolving instructions by priority and then by which instruction came later. If the result surprises you, inspect the computed style to see which rule won.

subtopics.title: Responsive styles
subtopics.explanation: CSS can change layout when available space changes. A media query applies rules under conditions such as a narrow viewport. It is like rearranging furniture when a room gets smaller. Combine flexible sizes with breakpoints when needed, and check that text, controls, and focus remain usable at zoom.

foundations.overview: CSS controls how HTML content looks and how it is arranged. A rule selects elements and gives them values for properties such as color, spacing, or layout. Think of HTML as the contents of a room and CSS as paint and furniture placement. Learn selectors and the cascade, then build responsive layouts that keep content readable at different sizes.
foundations.whyItMatters: CSS connects structure to readable, responsive presentation. Understanding how rules match and compete helps developers change a page without relying on brittle overrides.
commonUseCases: Set consistent spacing and color tokens for a design system.
Arrange cards into a responsive grid that changes at narrow widths.
Show keyboard focus clearly on links and buttons.
Define a consistent color, spacing, and typography system for an application.
Arrange cards responsively as the available screen space changes.
Show keyboard focus without changing the page’s semantic structure.
Use browser developer tools to inspect which selector wins for a component.
Check a responsive page at zoom and with longer translated copy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS only changes colors and decoration.
commonMisconceptions.reality: CSS controls layout, responsive behavior, animation, and visible focus as well as appearance.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The last rule in the file always wins.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Specificity, importance, and cascade layers can outrank later source order.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A desktop layout will shrink into a usable phone layout automatically.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Responsive rules and flexible sizing must account for narrow viewports and user zoom.

commonMisconceptions.myth: CSS is only decoration applied after a page is built.
commonMisconceptions.reality: CSS also determines layout, responsive behavior, focus visibility, and animation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Source order alone determines the winning rule.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Specificity, importance, and cascade layers also affect which declaration applies.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Responsive CSS is only for phone screen sizes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Zoom, text length, orientation, and available space can all change layout needs.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A valid CSS file means every declaration is applied.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unsupported or invalid values may be ignored, so inspect computed styles and target-browser behavior.

visualExplorer.title: How the browser turns CSS into pixels
visualExplorer.caption: Follow a stylesheet from text on disk to painted pixels on screen.

config.intro: CSS doesn't render directly — the browser parses it, matches it to elements, resolves conflicts, and only then paints.

steps.name: Parse HTML into the DOM
steps.detail: The browser reads HTML and builds a tree of elements (the DOM) representing the page structure.

steps.name: Parse CSS into rules (CSSOM)
steps.detail: Every ruleset is parsed into selectors and declarations, forming the CSS Object Model.

steps.name: Match selectors to elements
steps.detail: Each selector is tested against DOM elements to find which rules apply to which nodes.

steps.name: Resolve the cascade
steps.detail: When rules conflict, importance, specificity, and source order decide the winning value for each property.

steps.name: Compute final values
steps.detail: Relative values (like em or %) are resolved to absolute computed values used for layout.

steps.name: Layout and paint
steps.detail: The browser calculates positions and sizes, then paints colors, text, and borders to the screen.

interactiveExamples.title: Your first ruleset
interactiveExamples.explanation: An external stylesheet targets the heading and paragraph with simple rulesets that set color and font size.

files.index.html:
Hello, CSS

This paragraph is styled by an external stylesheet.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A blue heading and a dark-gray, comfortably spaced paragraph.

interactiveExamples.title: Three ways to apply CSS
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same page mixes external (link), internal (style tag), and inline (style attribute) CSS so you can see all three in action.

files.index.html:
External

Internal (style tag)

Inline (style attribute)

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A blue heading (external), a green line (internal), and a red line (inline).

codeLab.title: Style a card with an external stylesheet
codeLab.instructions: Write rulesets in styles.css so the .card has a white background, rounded corners, padding, and a subtle shadow, and the heading is blue. Edit only styles.css.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A white, rounded, padded card with a soft shadow and a blue heading.
hints: A ruleset is selector { property: value; }.
Use background, padding, border-radius, and box-shadow on .card, and color on .card h2.

keyTakeaways: A CSS rule has a selector and declarations.
A selector chooses which HTML elements receive a rule.
A property names the visual setting, such as `color`, `padding`, or `display`; its value tells the browser what to use.
The cascade decides which matching rule supplies a property when several rules apply.
CSS can change layout when available space changes.
